newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RB's Brash says working well with Treasurer Peters.
newsitem.headline: RB's Brash says working well with Treasurer Peters.

text.p: Reserve Bank of New Zealand governor Don Brash said on Thursday he had established a good working relationship with Treasurer Winston Peters.

"We have had absolutely no tension in our relationship," Brash told the New Zealand Press Association after releasing the bank's economic projection statement which took into account the coalition government's spending plans.
"We've had constructive meetings on several occasions.
"He clearly hasn't come from a university position where he has spent a long time studying monetary policy issues. But I think he is getting a very good grasp of the issues very quickly," Brash said.
Asked if Peters had ever challenged the idea of an independent central bank in meetings with him, Brash said: "He certainly hasn't with me at any time."
"I've had a good personal relationship with Mr Peters going back more than a decade and I don't have any difficulty dealing with him now at all."
Peters was critical of the effects of monetary policy in the election campaign last year and the coalition government document widened the bank's inflation target to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent.
Peters told a Treasury committee on Wednesday that the wider band made Brash's job easier and Brash agreed with that today.
Peters also told the committee yesterday he had an excellent relationship with Finance Minister Bill Birch and that the operation of the government's finance team was seamless.
Last week's budget policy statement said the government was committed to the inflation target and it had therefore avoided a rapid easing of fiscal policy.

The government plans to spend $5 billion extra over the next three years and the Reserve Bank incorporated those spending plans into today's forecasts saying that the government's plan contribute to a projected rise in inflation in late 1998 and 1999.

"The Government will need to be mindful of these inflationary risks in setting fiscal policy, particularly if there is no compulsory savings scheme to offset the impact of tax cuts currently planned for next year".
A referendum on a compulsory savings scheme is due in September.
